deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics: no formulas, computations or derivations. It is continuous prose from Riemann's natural-philosophical / psychological fragments, the argument for an 'Erdseele' (earth-soul). The page continues an argument begun on the previous folio.

Principle stated on the previous page: if a body of ponderable matter contains a closed system of continuing purpose-and-effect relations (Zweck- und Wirkungsbezüge), the most probable explanation is a unified ongoing thought-process (Denkprozess) inside that body. This holds provided (1) the purposiveness does not already close off within parts of the body, and (2) there is no reason to seek its cause in a larger whole to which the body belongs.

Application on this page. The organic purposiveness of organisms (their bodily design) is not explained by a thought-process inside the individual organism, for three reasons:
(1) It is not closed within the individual. The reasons for the design of the human organism lie in the constitution of the whole earth's surface, including organic nature.
(2) Organic motions repeat countless times, side by side in different individuals and successively in one individual or one lineage. So a common cause, not a separate one in each case, must be assumed.
(3) Organic designs undergo no further development within an individual's life (humans, animals) or within a generation (plants, embryos). So their cause is not a simultaneously running thought-process.

Individual purposiveness behaves differently. It is recognised in humans and animals, and perhaps occurs in plants. After subtracting the organic purposiveness, humans and animals (and plants, on 'F.'s' view) retain a closed system of interlocking, changeable purpose-effect relations. This is to be explained by a unified thought-process within them, and inner perception confirms it.

By the same principles, the cause of organic purposiveness must be sought in a unified thought-process in the Earth:
(a) Purpose-effect relations in terrestrial organic life do not split into separate systems; everything interlocks. So several partial thought-processes in parts of the Earth cannot explain them.
(b) As far as experience reaches, there is no reason to look to a larger whole. Reason (b)1 is that this purposiveness closes off within the Earth: all organisms are made only for life on the earth's crust. Reasons (b)2-3 continue on the next page: organisms are individual to the Earth, and they progress over the Earth's history.

The conclusion, drawn on the next page, is that the earth-soul is a hypothesis of explanatory natural science.

I cannot restate any derivation in modern notation, because there is none.
errors: The argument is a qualitative inference to the best explanation. Its premises are period-bound: for example, that organic designs undergo 'no further development' within the life of a lineage, and that organisms are 'only' adapted to Earth. These are philosophical or empirical assumptions, not logical errors.

results.what: Teleological argument for a unified 'earth-soul' thought-process as the cause of organic purposiveness, distinguished from individual souls (Denkprozesse) in humans, animals and possibly plants.
results.usually_credited_to: Gustav Theodor Fechner (Nanna, 1848; Zend-Avesta, 1851), whose views Riemann adopts and reworks

deep.surprise_reason: Purely philosophical prose with no mathematics. Riemann's Fechner-inspired Erdseele argument from his natural-philosophy fragments is known. It was published, partly edited, in the 'Fragmente philosophischen Inhalts' of the Gesammelte Werke (Weber/Dedekind, 1876). The pencil note 'Von hier an weggelassen' on the next page reflects that editorial preparation.
transcription_corrections: 'bei den Pflanzen nach F.s[?] Ansicht': the initial is hard to read in the image (it could be read as 'S.s'). From context (the plant-soul doctrine), the person meant is almost certainly Fechner (Nanna oder über das Seelenleben der Pflanzen).
The circled '22' in the right margin is the folio/sheet number of the bundle, not part of the text; '43' at the top is the page number.
Line 'für (an) sich schon liegt': 'an' is written above/beside 'für' as an alternative, rendered correctly as a variant.

Minor orthographic points: the manuscript uses 'ß'/'ss' inconsistently (e.g. 'anerkanntermaßen', 'grösseren'). The transcription normalises some of these, and its hyphenated 'anerkannter-maßen' is just a line break.
